Henry P. Leifermann reported for United Press International from Memphis on an unusual demand. Humbert James Putt, a federal prisoner, insisted on testifying in the trial of James Earl Ray. A court had ruled Putt mentally incompetent. His claims touched both the King and Kennedy assassinations, and the wire described them as bizarre.

Big cases attract claimants from every margin, and Ray's trial drew its share. A prisoner demanding the stand with tales of two assassinations tested the court's patience and the wire's restraint. Leifermann's report preserves the episode as Memphis read it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MullenRobertRud:
Ron Rosenbaum wrote 'Wallowing in Watergate' about a document the Ervin Committee never released. The committee's staff had prepared a 46-page study of connections between Howard Hughes and Larry O'Brien. O'Brien chaired the Democratic National Committee, whose headquarters were burgled in the Watergate break-in. The study was deleted from the committee's output.

Rosenbaum asks why a finished staff study on Hughes and O'Brien was buried. Hughes money moved through the politics of both parties, and O'Brien had worked for Hughes. The article follows the deleted study as a story inside the larger scandal: work done, then suppressed, then reported on anyway. It is Watergate told through one missing document.

lenin-development-capitalism-russia-1899:
Lenin wrote The Development of Capitalism in Russia in 1899, signing it with the name Vladimir Ilyin. The Russian original is the text held here. Narodnik writers had claimed that capitalism could not take root in peasant Russia. Lenin answers them with a mass of Russian statistics.

He shows markets, wage labor, and class splits already growing inside the village. That evidence formed the empirical base of Russian Marxism. The book grew from his Siberian exile studies and prison work. No public domain English translation exists, so the Russian stands alone. Readers with Russian meet the young Lenin as researcher.
